summary: Specifies an extension to IEEE 802.11 for opportunistic, unauthenticated encryption of wireless traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: Opportunistic Wireless Encryption gives an open Wi-Fi connection encryption without asking the user for a password. It does not verify the identity of the access point, so it cannot stop an active attacker from pretending to be one.

subtitle: Wireless encryption for open Wi-Fi that does not require a shared password.

tldr.problem: Open Wi-Fi exposes traffic to passive observers, while a public shared password does not keep traffic secret from people who know that password.
tldr.mechanism: The client and access point exchange Diffie-Hellman public keys during association, derive a Pairwise Master Key and use the normal 4-way handshake to create traffic keys.
tldr.outcome: OWE encrypts the wireless link without authenticating either side. RFC 8110 is Informational and was updated by RFC 9672.

today: RFC 8110 is Informational and was updated by RFC 9672. It specifies encryption without authentication.

sections.title: Why Encrypt Open Wi-Fi
sections.content:
Open wireless networks do not encrypt traffic over the wireless link, which leaves it open to passive observation. A public shared Pre-Shared Key does not solve this problem because an observer who knows the key can derive traffic keys from the 4-way handshake.

OWE adds unauthenticated encryption without requiring special configuration or user interaction. It is intended to provide more protection than an open network or a shared public key, not to identify the access point.
sections.plainLanguage: A public Wi-Fi password cannot keep traffic secret from people who also know that password. OWE creates fresh encryption keys for a connection without requiring the user to enter one.

sections.title: Diffie-Hellman Key Agreement
sections.content:
OWE uses a Diffie-Hellman exchange to derive a shared secret between the client and access point. The exchange uses a group identifier that selects the domain parameters and supports elliptic-curve and finite-field groups.

The RFC requires implementations to support group 19, a 256-bit elliptic-curve group. A hash algorithm is selected according to the group parameters and is used to derive the secret and its identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and access point exchange public values and independently derive the same secret. The RFC requires support for one specific elliptic-curve group so implementations can interoperate.

sections.title: Discovery and Association
sections.content:
An access point advertises OWE support in its RSN element in beacons and probe responses. A client that selects OWE uses Open System authentication and then includes a Diffie-Hellman Parameter element in its association request.

The access point returns its public key in the association response. If it cannot use the requested group, it responds with status code 77, and the client should retry with another supported group. Invalid received keys cause association to fail.
sections.plainLanguage: The access point advertises that it supports OWE. During association, the client and access point exchange the public values used to derive their shared secret.

sections.title: Deriving Keys and Protecting Traffic
sections.content:
After association, both sides use the Diffie-Hellman result and HKDF to derive a Pairwise Master Key and its identifier. The RFC says the intermediate secret values should be irretrievably deleted after the PMK is generated.

The access point then starts the normal 4-way handshake using that PMK. The handshake generates keys to protect unicast and broadcast data over the wireless link. PMK caching can let a client and access point reuse a cached PMK on a later association.
sections.plainLanguage: The shared secret is converted into a Pairwise Master Key. The usual 4-way handshake then derives the keys that protect data sent over the wireless link.

sections.title: Encryption Without Authentication
sections.content:
OWE does not authenticate the client or access point. It gives them shared traffic keys and protection against changes to frames in transit, but an active attacker can impersonate an access point and relay traffic to the legitimate one.

OWE protects only the wireless medium, not end-to-end traffic. The RFC says it is not a replacement for an 802.11 authentication protocol and is not intended where an authenticated alternative is available.
sections.plainLanguage: OWE encrypts the wireless connection but does not tell the client who controls the access point. Use end-to-end security for application traffic, and use an authentication method when one is available.

references.text: Dukhovni, V., "Opportunistic Security: Some Protection Most of the Time", RFC 7435, December 2014.
